stem: The earliest surviving manuscript paintings in India were made on __________.
solution: Early Indian manuscript paintings were done on palm leaves before paper became common.

stem: The eastern Indian manuscript painting tradition flourished under the __________ dynasty.
solution: The Pala dynasty of eastern India patronised the earliest Buddhist manuscript painting.

stem: The Pala manuscript paintings were mostly __________ in theme.
solution: Pala manuscript paintings mainly illustrated Buddhist texts.

stem: A famous Buddhist text illustrated in the Pala style is the __________.
solution: The Ashtasahasrika Prajnaparamita was a key Buddhist text illustrated in Pala manuscripts.

stem: The western Indian manuscript tradition was largely associated with __________ texts.
solution: The western Indian school mainly illustrated Jain religious texts.

stem: The Jain manuscript painting tradition flourished mainly in the region of __________.
solution: The western Indian (Jain) style flourished in Gujarat and Rajasthan.

stem: A well-known Jain text that was frequently illustrated is the __________.
solution: The Jain Kalpasutra was one of the most illustrated western Indian manuscripts.

stem: A distinctive feature of western Indian (Jain) manuscript figures is the __________.
options: projecting (further) eye seen in profile faces
solution: Figures in profile show a characteristic projecting 'further eye'.

stem: The introduction of __________ from the 14th–15th centuries changed the size and format of manuscript painting.
solution: The arrival of paper allowed larger formats and more elaborate manuscript paintings.

stem: The colours used in early manuscript paintings were mostly __________.
solution: Manuscript paintings used natural mineral and vegetable pigments.

stem: The palm-leaf manuscripts were bound and protected by wooden covers called __________.
solution: Palm-leaf manuscripts were protected by painted wooden covers (patli).

stem: Manuscript illustrations were meant to __________ the sacred text.
solution: The illustrations accompanied and illuminated the religious text.

stem: The Gujarat/western Indian style later blended with __________ influences to form early Rajput/Sultanate painting.
solution: The western Indian style absorbed Persian influences, contributing to later Rajput and Sultanate painting.

stem: The 'Kalpasutra' illustrated at Mandu and Jaunpur shows the spread of the __________ style.
solution: Illustrated Kalpasutras at Mandu and Jaunpur show the spread of the western Indian style.

stem: The Pala style of painting came to an end largely due to the __________.
options: destruction of Buddhist monasteries in the 12th–13th centuries
solution: The Pala tradition declined after the destruction of Buddhist monasteries in eastern India.

stem: Manuscript painting was a __________ art form, meant to be viewed closely.
solution: Manuscript painting is a miniature art form meant for close viewing.

stem: The Buddhist manuscript paintings of the Pala school influenced the art of __________.
solution: The Pala Buddhist painting style influenced Nepal and Tibet.

stem: The manuscripts were written and painted by __________.
options: scribes and artists in monasteries and workshops
solution: Scribes and artists in monasteries and workshops produced illustrated manuscripts.

stem: The colours in Jain manuscripts became richer with the use of __________ and lapis blue on paper.
solution: Later Jain manuscripts used lavish gold and ultramarine (lapis) blue.

stem: The illustrated 'Gita Govinda' and 'Chaurapanchasika' belong to a group of __________ manuscripts.
solution: The Gita Govinda and Chaurapanchasika are early Hindu (pre-Mughal Rajput) illustrated manuscripts.

stem: The 'Chaurapanchasika' style is important as a forerunner of __________ painting.
solution: The Chaurapanchasika group is a key forerunner of Rajasthani (Rajput) painting.

stem: In manuscript paintings, the space for the picture was usually left within the __________.
solution: Illustrations were painted within spaces left on the written manuscript page.

stem: The figures in Pala paintings are marked by __________ lines and simple compositions.
solution: Pala paintings show graceful, flowing lines and restrained compositions.

stem: The transition from palm leaf to paper allowed artists to paint __________ compositions.
solution: Paper allowed larger and more detailed compositions than narrow palm leaves.

stem: The western Indian style is sometimes called the __________ style.
solution: The western Indian manuscript style is also called the Apabhramsa or Gujarat style.

stem: Manuscript painting forms the __________ of the later Indian miniature painting tradition.
solution: The manuscript tradition is the foundation of later Indian miniature painting.

stem: The illustrations in Buddhist manuscripts often depicted __________.
options: deities and scenes from the Buddha's life
solution: Buddhist manuscript paintings depict deities and scenes from the Buddha's life.

stem: The stylised, angular figures with pointed noses are typical of the __________ manuscript style.
solution: Western Indian (Jain) figures are stylised, angular, with pointed noses and the projecting eye.

stem: The colours red and __________ dominate the backgrounds of many western Indian Jain manuscripts.
solution: Rich red and ultramarine blue backgrounds are typical of western Indian Jain manuscripts.

stem: The manuscript painting tradition shows a shift from __________ to secular and courtly themes over time.
solution: Over time the tradition expanded from purely religious to secular and courtly themes.

stem: The Jain community's role in commissioning manuscripts reflects the importance of __________ in art patronage.
solution: Prosperous Jain merchant communities were important patrons of manuscript painting.

stem: The vibrant, flat colours and lack of deep perspective in manuscript painting reflect its __________.
solution: Manuscript painting favours flat colour and a decorative, two-dimensional aesthetic.

stem: The manuscript tradition of eastern and western India developed __________.
options: in parallel, with different religious themes
solution: The eastern (Pala/Buddhist) and western (Jain) traditions developed in parallel with different themes.

stem: The manuscript illustrations were valued for both their __________.
solution: Illustrated manuscripts were prized for religious merit and artistic beauty.

stem: The narrow horizontal format of early manuscript paintings was determined by the shape of the __________.
solution: The long narrow format followed the shape of the palm leaf.

stem: A characteristic red or blue background dot pattern and floral borders appear in __________ manuscripts.
solution: Later paper Jain manuscripts show decorative borders and patterned backgrounds.

stem: The 'further eye' convention means the eye on the far side of a profile face is __________.
solution: The far eye is shown projecting beyond the facial outline in western Indian painting.

stem: The manuscript tradition demonstrates the close link between __________ and painting in medieval India.
solution: Manuscript painting shows the close link between religious text and painting.

stem: The Pala and western Indian styles are important as the __________ phase of Indian miniature painting.
solution: These form the earliest phase of the Indian miniature painting tradition.

stem: Which of the following materials was NOT typically used as a support for early manuscript painting?
solution: Canvas was not used; supports were palm leaf, paper and wooden covers.

stem: The manuscript painters worked in a style that emphasised __________ over naturalism.
solution: Manuscript painting emphasised convention and symbolism rather than naturalism.

stem: The illustrated manuscript was usually meant for __________ use.
solution: Illustrated manuscripts were used for religious study and worship.

stem: The western Indian style is significant because it survived and evolved even under __________ rule.
solution: The western Indian style continued and evolved under the Delhi Sultanate.

stem: The manuscript painting tradition ultimately fed into the great schools of __________ painting.
solution: The manuscript tradition fed into the Rajput and Mughal miniature schools.

stem: The colours in Pala paintings tend to be __________ compared with the bold western Indian palette.
solution: Pala painting uses softer, subdued colours compared with the bold western Indian palette.

stem: The main patrons of the western Indian manuscript tradition were the __________.
solution: Jain merchant families and monastic orders were the chief patrons.

stem: The manuscript illustrations help historians study the __________ of medieval India.
solution: The illustrations reveal medieval Indian dress, ornament and religious life.

stem: The manuscript painting tradition spanned roughly the __________ centuries.
solution: The manuscript painting tradition flourished roughly between the 10th and 15th centuries.

stem: The key achievement of the manuscript tradition was preserving and transmitting __________ through art.
solution: It preserved and transmitted religious and literary knowledge through illustration.

stem: The gradual replacement of palm leaf by paper marks a __________ in the manuscript tradition.
solution: The shift from palm leaf to paper was a major technical turning point.
